text: At the end of pretraining you have a model that has read a small library, yet if you ask it a question it may simply write three more questions, because on the web a question is often followed by others of its kind. The knowledge is in there; what is missing is the habit of answering. Fine-tuning is how that habit is taught, and the surprising part is how little has to change.

Fine-tuning means continuing to train the same network, with the same next-token loss, on a much smaller and carefully chosen set of examples. Think of a trained pianist learning a new piece: the hands and the ear are already there, so light practice is enough, while hours of forceful drilling on one piece can make the others slip away. That is why fine-tuning uses a small learning rate and relatively few steps, since large updates can erase what pretraining built, an effect called catastrophic forgetting.

For instruction tuning, each example is a conversation written out as one long text, with special tokens marking where the user's turn ends and the assistant's turn begins. The model reads the whole conversation, but the loss is usually counted only on the assistant's tokens. Each token's loss is multiplied by a mask of ones and zeros, so the model is graded on producing answers, not on imitating the questions.

In twenty twenty-one, Wei and colleagues at Google fine-tuned a large model on many different tasks, each one phrased as a plain instruction. Their model, called FLAN, became better at following instructions for kinds of task it had never been tuned on, which suggests that it learned the general pattern of doing what an instruction asks, not just the individual tasks.

OpenAI's InstructGPT used the same recipe as its first step, with demonstrations written by trained human labellers. The paper reports about thirteen thousand training prompts for that stage, a tiny amount next to the hundreds of billions of tokens the base model had already read, which shows how much of the work pretraining had done.

Updating every weight is expensive, because every tuned copy of a large model is itself large. LoRA, from Hu and colleagues at Microsoft, freezes the original weight matrix and learns a correction that is the product of two thin matrices, called B and A. For a square matrix four thousand wide and a rank of eight, the two thin strips hold a few tens of thousands of numbers instead of almost seventeen million. And because B starts at zero, the tuned model begins exactly where the pretrained one left off.

Why should such a narrow correction be enough? The LoRA authors hypothesised that the change fine-tuning needs has a low intrinsic rank, meaning it lives in a handful of directions, much as the colour balance of a photograph can be changed everywhere at once with only a few dials, and their experiments supported it, with very small ranks performing well. A practical bonus is that one frozen base model can carry many small adapters, swapped in for different tasks.

So fine-tuning teaches format and behaviour from a modest set of examples, while the knowledge comes mostly from pretraining. Demonstrations, however, show one good answer at a time, and they cannot easily say which of two answers is better. Learning from those comparisons is the subject of the next lesson, on learning from human preferences.
